title: The four cases
goal: Know what each case does and decline the definite article.

blocks.text: Greek nouns, adjectives, articles and pronouns change their endings for **case**, which shows the job a word does in the sentence. There are four: nominative, accusative, genitive and vocative. Because the article changes with case, it is often the clearest signal: **ο** φίλος (subject), **τον** φίλο (object), **του** φίλου (of the friend).

blocks.title: The definite article
blocks.cite: Holton §3.4. The vocative has no article.

blocks.text: Notice how few distinct forms there are: **του** is masculine and neuter genitive singular, **των** is every genitive plural, and **τα** covers neuter nominative and accusative plural. Feminine accusative **τη(ν)** keeps its ν before a vowel and before κ, π, τ, γκ, μπ, ντ, ξ, ψ: την άνοιξη, την πόρτα, but τη Δευτέρα.

blocks.title: Street names in the genitive
blocks.text: Greek addresses are a daily genitive drill. A street is usually 'the street **of** someone': **οδός Ερμού** 'Hermes Street' (literally 'street of Hermes'), **Πλατεία Συντάγματος** 'Syntagma (Constitution) Square', **Λεωφόρος Βασιλίσσης Σοφίας** 'Queen Sophia Avenue'. In speech the word οδός drops out but its feminine article stays, so people say **Μένω στην Ερμού** or **στην Πατησίων**. On envelopes and maps you will also see the abbreviations **Λεωφ.** for λεωφόρος 'avenue' and **Πλ.** for πλατεία 'square'.

blocks.title: σε + article
head: σε + article
Contracted
blocks.cite: Holton §3.4. σε 'to, in, at' always fuses with a following definite article.

items.why: Before a vowel the ν stays: στην Αθήνα.

items.prompt: Δίνω το βιβλίο ___ φίλους μου. (σε + τους)

items.why: The subject of the verb is in the nominative.
The direct object is in the accusative.
Possession ('of') is the genitive.
Feminine subject: nominative η.
Feminine genitive singular: της.
Every genitive plural, in all genders, is των.
Feminine accusative plural is τις; τους is masculine.

items.prompt: **Γιάννη**, έλα εδώ! Which case is Γιάννη?
items.why: Addressing someone directly is the vocative, used without an article.
The owner goes after the noun in the genitive: του φίλου.
σε fuses with το: στο.
Feminine accusative τη(ν); before γ the ν is normally dropped.
σε + τη(ν) = στη(ν); before μ the ν is normally dropped.
Genitive plural article: των.
Before a vowel the ν must stay: στην Ελένη.

items.prompt: Say in Greek: *in the cities* (η πόλη, pl. οι πόλεις)
items.why: σε + τις = στις; feminine accusative plural.
Feminine genitive: της μητέρας.
Masculine accusative plural: τους.
Before π the ν stays: την πόρτα.
The possessor is genitive plural: των παιδιών.
Before θ the ν is normally dropped: στη Θεσσαλονίκη.
